title: The Moon
summary: A sharp, detailed Moon with a long lens.

media.alt: Full Moon in detail against a black sky

blocks.note: Full Moon rule of thumb: f/11 at 1/ISO (ISO 100, 1/125 s).

blocks.alt: The eight Moon phases from new to waning crescent
blocks.caption: The best crater detail is along the shadow line, so crescents and quarters beat a full Moon.

steps: Pick a clear night. A crescent or quarter Moon shows craters; a full Moon looks flat but bright.
Longest lens on a tripod. On an APS-C camera a 250 mm lens frames like 400 mm.
Manual mode: f/8, ISO 100, 1/125 s. The Moon is lit by the sun, so it needs daytime settings.
Manual focus: magnify the live view on the Moon's edge and turn the ring until craters are crisp.
Use the 2 s timer and take a test shot. Check the histogram: the bright side must not touch the right wall.
Take a burst of 10–20 frames. Air shimmer makes some sharper than others; keep the best.

items: A low Moon near the horizon looks big next to buildings or hills, but blurs more through the air.
Want the Moon and a landscape? Shoot at blue hour, when the sky and the Moon are close in brightness.
The Moon moves. Above 400 mm keep the shutter at 1/125 s or faster.

steps: Switch to **MF**. Magnify the live view on the Moon's edge and focus on the craters.
**MENU › Shooting 7 › Drive mode › Self-timer: 2 sec** (or the BR-E1 remote).
Lens IS off on the tripod: the R10 has no in-body stabiliser, so the lens switch is the one that matters.
Take a test shot and check the histogram. Turn on **Playback 5 › Highlight alert** to see blown highlights blink.
Switch to **continuous shooting** in the drive mode menu and take a burst. Keep the sharpest frame.
canon-r10.note: With a 300 mm lens the R10's crop makes it frame like 480 mm, which fills about a third of the frame height with the Moon.
